summary: The note argues that zero-waste cooking is an urgent necessity for regional kitchens and that policy change is needed to support it. It surveys chefs and organizations using nose-to-tail cooking, farm-to-fork sourcing, surplus donation, software and compost technology, and traditional whole-ingredient recipes. It closes by calling for tax incentives, composting subsidies and legislative frameworks.
one_line: Regional chefs, nonprofits and technology are advancing zero-waste cooking, and the note argues policy incentives and legislation are needed to make it standard.
key_facts: According to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, about one-third of food produced for human consumption, roughly 1.3 billion tons, is lost or wasted each year.
On November 2, 2023, Chef Amanda Richardson of the bistro "Harvest Table" in Smithfield said that kitchens disregarding their waste are part of 'a deeper ethical crisis.'
Chef Peter Lowell of "The Foraged Truffle" in Monroe, Ohio uses a nose-to-tail approach; he uses beet roots for entrees, stems for pickling and greens in salads.
Chef Emily Santos of Asheville, North Carolina has pioneered a farm-to-fork philosophy since late September 2023, which cuts transport emissions and packaging waste.
"Greens that Give" was founded on October 15, 2023 by environmental activist Jacob Martin; it connects local farmers with restaurants and sends surplus to food banks.
The "Conscious Cuisine Conference" was held December 3, 2023 in Portland to raise awareness of food waste and educate policy-makers.
Policy-makers are urged to offer tax incentives for zero-waste restaurants and subsidies for composting programs and waste reduction, to help smaller independent kitchens.
The software "WasteNot," launched September 9, 2023, helps restaurant managers track food usage and purchase patterns to prevent overordering.
"The Urban Tiller" in San Francisco uses high-tech compost machines that break down food scraps within 24 hours into nutrient-rich soil for its herb gardens.
Chef Rafaela Diaz of "La Tradición" in El Paso, Texas uses leftover corn husks for tamales and whips chickpea water into aquafaba as a vegan egg replacement.
Overstocked pantries and poor meal planning are named as common kitchen habits that lead food to landfill.
The note calls for continuous dialogue among chefs, consumers, environmentalists and legislators to build a framework that rewards sustainable practices.
